            HABITAT CONTROL
            1.     Brush Management. (2026-2030) Brush management is an effective tool for controlling
                   encroachment of regrowth Ashe juniper and fostering the production of desirable trees, shrubs,
                   grasses, and forbs, which promotes forage, nesting, and/or protective cover for songbirds, deer,
                   small mammals, Wild turkey, quail, and other native wildlife species. The landowners will selectively
                   remove excessive brush from entire property.
                   Best practices for controlling excess brush and mitigating risk of reinvasion include:
                     • Assessing soil types, slope angle and direction to minimize soil loss and erosion
                     • Targeting juniper in its early growth stage with hand loppers and/or chainsaws
                     • Removing juniper shorter than 8 feet and with a main trunk diameter that measures 6 inches
                       or less at breast height

                   In addition, the landowners will selectively remove overgrowth of prickly pear throughout to reduce

                   Best practices for controlling prickly pear and mitigating risk of reinvasion include:
                         •   Allowing cactus occurring in diverse brush mottes to stand
                         •   Targeting cactus occurring by themselves or in limited-diversity mottes, e.g., those
                             inhabited by only mesquite and cactus
                         •   Using a tractor loading bucket to grub cactus and its root system out of the ground
                         •   Supplementing mechanical treatment with chemical control
                         •   Avoiding the spread of prickly pear pads during treatment, which will exacerbate invasion

                   The landowners will annually conduct brush management activities on a minimum of 10% of the 34-

            PREDATOR CONTROL
            1.     Predator Management. (2026-2030) The landowners will control raccoons and coyotes, which are
                   known to occur in the area and have caused problems on the property. These native, opportunistic
                   predators are a natural part of the ecosystem. In some cases, however, these species can greatly
                   overpopulate and pose a significant threat to native wildlife populations, if dependable water and
                   food sources (e.g., feeders) are accessible to them threatening ground-nesting birds and small
                   mammals, such as rabbits.
                   The landowners will maintain annual documentation, to include predator harvest, photos, invoices,
                   map of trap location(s) (if applicable), and other associated monitoring records that can be made
                   available to the county upon request. The landowners will place baited live-traps near known
                   concentrations of the varmints as often as possible, primarily in spring and early summer months.
                   The landowners will record and evaluate incidental sightings of predators annually to determine
                   when to scale back control measures. The landowners will maintain annual documentation, to
                   include predator harvest logs, photos, map of trap location(s) (if applicable), and other associated
                   monitoring records that can be made available to the county upon request.
            2.     Imported Red Fire Ant (IRFA) Control. (2026-2030) The landowners will develop and execute a
                   predator management plan to reduce the presence of Imported Red Fire Ants (IRFA), which are

            1.     Well/Trough/Windmill Overflow/Other Wildlife Watering Devices. (2026-2030) Water is an essential

            PROVIDING SUPPLEMENTAL SUPPLIES OF FOOD
            1.     Feeders and Mineral Supplementation. (2026-2030) Reliable food resources are essential for
                   wildlife. While a healthy and diverse habitat provides natural sources of food, supplying
                   supplemental sources can encourage wildlife survival and propagation, particularly during breeding
                   seasons and periods of harsh weather. Protein is an important form of a white-tailed deer diet that
                   can improve antler mass and body condition. The landowners will maintain 2 feeders to provide
                   wildlife with a reliable source of protein on a year-round basis, which exceeds TPWD’s minimum
                   requirement of one feeder per 320 acres.
                   Best practices for protein supplementation include:
                     • Use commercial protein pellets, alfalfa pellets, soybeans, peas, or whole cottonseed
                     • Avoid providing only corn, which lacks nutritional value and does not qualify as a supplemental
                       food source
                     • Avoid spin-cast, timed feeders, as they do not satisfy TPWD requirements for this wildlife
                       management activity
                     • Clean and fill feeders regularly
                   With low to moderately low deer densities, the presence of supplemental food will increase the
                   nutritional plane of deer. The landowners will maintain annual documentation to include feed

            1.     Nest Boxes, Bat Boxes. (2026-2030) Providing supplemental shelter for cavity-nesting wildlife

                         •   Monitor annually for predators, occupancy, and successful breeding

                   desirable shrubs and/or trees, such as live oak and cedar elm, protect them from deer browsing,
                   promoting regeneration and growth.
                   Best practices for brush pile construction include:
                     • Place brush piles in areas that lack sufficient cover-providing shrubs
                     • Shape brush piles into mounds or teepees 6-8 feet high and 10-15 feet in diameter
                     • Form the base of the brush pile with the largest material, such as trunks or logs, and apply
                       layers of smaller limbs and branches as filler
                     • Create an open cavity at the base of each pile to promote animal access
                     • Reshape and maintain existing brush piles annually, as an alternative to new construction
                   The landowners will retain applicable annual documentation, such as a map of brush pile locations

9 Date: May 20, 2020

A breeding bird survey was conducted on the Prang property in Bell County on the morning of May 20,
2020. James A. Hall, biologist for Plateau Land and Wildlife, conducted the survey. The protocol for
the survey was to re-survey or establish stations throughout the 24.21 acre ranch at 250 meter (.15 mile)
or greater intervals. Observations, both visual and auditory, were taken at each station for periods
lasting three minutes. We observed 4 station(s) during this survey. The survey began at 0708 and ended
at 0803. Weather conditions were noted at the beginning and end of the survey.

An annual survey using the same stations will be conducted on the property during the breeding season
(mid March - mid June), between 0600 and 1100 hours. These surveys will be helpful in determining
trends in population changes of the breeding birds on the subject property. This information could be
useful in targeting and/or maintaining management activities with regards to breeding birds found on
the Prang property.

A brief description of the stations, beginning and ending weather observations, and a list of bird
observations organized by station follows.

Station 1

The first station is located in the northern end of the property, near the site of the "barndominium". The
surrounding habitat consists of open oak savannah, with scattered live oaks and the occasional elm and
hackberry. The shrub layer contains mostly juniper, persimmon, prickly pear, agarita, and greenbriar,
and the ground is dominated by native grasses such as bluestem, muhly, grama, and interspersed
wildflowers. A total of 7 species were observed.

Station 2

Station 2 is situated on the dam of a new pond, constructed within a formerly boggy section of the
western drainage. The surrounding habitat is consistent with what's found at Station 1, which is
thematic across the property. However, the drainage corridor contains a greater diversity of shrubby
species (elbowbush, yaupon, wafer ash, redbud, elm, and bumelia). Most-soil sedges and weedy forbs
are common in the vicinity. A total of 12 species were observed.

Station 3

Station 3 can be found near the far southern corner of the property, on a limestone ledge overlooking
the landscape which continues to decline to the south onto neighboring properties. The habitat is
consistent with live oak savannah. A total of 8 species were observed.

 Station 4

The fourth station is found along the eastern boundary, again within the open savannah habitat, along
one of the old unimproved ranch roads. Many of the live oaks visible from here are very large and
healthy specimens, containing a mix of understory shrubs. A total of 9 species were observed.

             PREDATOR CONTROL
             1.    Predator Management. (2026-2030) The landowners will control raccoons and coyotes, which are

                   predators are a natural part of the ecosystem. In some cases, however, these species can greatly
                   overpopulate and pose a significant threat to native wildlife populations, if dependable water and
                   food sources (e.g., feeders) are accessible to them threatening ground-nesting birds and small
                   mammals, such as rabbits.
                   The landowners will maintain annual documentation, to include predator harvest, photos, invoices,
                   map of trap location(s) (if applicable), and other associated monitoring records that can be made
                   available to the county upon request. The landowners will place baited live-traps near known
                   concentrations of the varmints as often as possible, primarily in spring and early summer months.
                   The landowners will record and evaluate incidental sightings of predators annually to determine
                   when to scale back control measures. The landowners will maintain annual documentation, to
                   include predator harvest logs, photos, map of trap location(s) (if applicable), and other associated
                   monitoring records that can be made available to the county upon request.
             2.    Imported Red Fire Ant (IRFA) Control. (2026-2030) The landowners will develop and execute a

             1.    Well/TroughA/Vindmill Overflow/Other Wildlife Watering Devices. (2026-2030) Water is an essential

                   drowning while using the watering device. Drowning can easily be averted by constructing a simple
                   ramp of rocks, wire, Iumber, or other material on the internal and external sides of each watering
                   device, allowing safe access and escape for all wildlife species. Ideal placement of supplemental
                   water includes areas that are lacking a pond, creek, river, or other natural water source, and in

                   separate supplemental water sources.

             PROVIDING SUPPLEMENTAL SUPPLIES OF FooD
             1.    Feeders and Mineral Supplementation. (2026-2030) Reliable food resources are essential for
                   wildlife. While a healthy and diverse habitat provides natural sources of food, supplying
                   supplemental sources can encourage wildlife survival and propagation, particularly during breeding
                   seasons and periods of harsh weather. Protein is an important form of a white-tailed deer diet that
                   can improve antler mass and body condition. The landowners will maintain 2 feeders to provide
                   wildlife with a reliable source of protein on a year-round basis, which exceeds TPWD's minimum
                   requirement of one feeder per 320 acres.
                   Best practices for protein supplementation include:
                     •   Use commercial protein pellets, alfalfa pellets, soybeans, peas, or whole cottonseed
                     •   Avoid providing only corn, which lacks nutritional value and does not qualify as a supplemental
                         food source
                     •   Avoid spin-cast, timed feeders, as they do not satisfy TPWD requirements for this wildlife
                         management activity
                     •   Clean and fill feeders regularly

  Management                                                                   Date: May 20,2020

A breeding bird survey was conducted on the Prang property in Bell County on the morning of May 20,
2020. James A. Hall, biologist for Plateau Land and Wildlife, conducted the survey. The protocol for
the survey was to re-survey or establish stations throughout the 24.21 acre ranch at 250 meter (.15 mile)
or greater intervals. Observations, both visual and auditory, were taken at each station for periods
lasting three minutes. We observed 4 station(s) during this survey. The survey began at 0708 and ended
at 0803. Weather conditions were noted at the beginning and end of the survey.

An annual survey using the same stations will be conducted on the property during the breeding season
(mid March - mid June), between 0600 and 1100 hours. These surveys will be helpful in determining
trends in population changes of the breeding birds on the subject property. This information could be
useful in targeting and/or maintaining management activities with regards to breeding birds found on
the Prang property.

A brief description of the stations, beginning and ending weather observations, and a list of bird
observations organized by station follows.

Station 1
The first station is located in the northern end of the property, near the site of the "barndominium". The
surrounding habitat consists of open oak savannah, with scattered live oaks and the occasional elm and
hackberry. The shrub layer contains mostly juniper, persimmon, prickly pear, agarita, and greenbriar,
and the ground is dominated by native grasses such as bluestem, muhly, grama, and interspersed
wildflowers. A total of 7 species were observed.



Station 2
Station 2 is situated on the dam of a new pond, constructed within a formerly boggy section of the
western drainage. The surrounding habitat is consistent with what's found at Station 1, which is
thematic across the property. However, the drainage corridor contains a greater diversity of shrubby
species (elbowbush, yaupon, wafer ash, redbud, elm, and bumelia). Most-soil sedges and weedy forbs
are common in the vicinity. A total of 12 species were observed.



Station 3
Station 3 can be found near the far southern corner of the property, on a limestone ledge overlooking
the landscape which continues to decline to the south onto neighboring properties. The habitat is
consistent with live oak savannah. A total of 8 species were observed.
 Station 4
The fourth station is found along the eastern boundary, again within the open savannah habitat, along
one ofthe old unimproved ranch roads. Many of the live oaks visible from here are very large and
healthy specimens, containing a mix of understory shrubs. A total of 9 species were observed.
